title: Malachi
subtitle: the last prophet's six arguments with a tired people
lead: Malachi is the last book of the Twelve and, in the Christian Bible, the last of the Old Testament. It speaks to the priests and people of the small Persian province of Judah, some decades after the Temple was rebuilt. The glory that Haggai and Zechariah promised had not come. The harvests were poor, the Persian governor was in charge, and many people were saying it was pointless to serve God. Malachi answers in a form no other prophet uses so steadily: six arguments, each with a charge, an objection and a reply, the objection always starting with 'But you say.'

The topics are love and election (Jacob and Esau), polluted offerings, the covenant with Levi, betrayal in marriage and divorce, the God of justice, the tithe, and the day that burns like an oven and heals like the sun. The book ends with two commands that look in two directions: remember the law of Moses, and watch for Elijah. The New Testament opens its story of John the Baptist with them (Matthew 11:10-14; Luke 1:17).
facts: Author

Unknown. 'Malachi' means 'my messenger' (see 3:1), and many scholars think it is the book's title and not the prophet's name. The Targum Jonathan says he was Ezra the scribe, and Jerome also discusses the identification with Ezra; the Talmud (Megillah 15a) records views that he was Mordecai, that he was Ezra, and that Malachi was his real name. Others accept Malachi as a real name.
Date

In the Persian period, after the Temple was finished in about 515 BC. Proposed dates run from about 480 to 435 BC, many near 450 BC; some bring it close to Nehemiah's second term (about 432 BC). The views are in 'Date and setting' below.
Setting
Jerusalem and the Persian province of Judah (Hebrew Yehud) under a governor (1:8), with the Temple working and the priests receiving the people's offerings.
Kind of writing

Prose-and-poetry disputation. Modern editions differ on which lines are verse (often 1:11, 3:1-4 and 4:1-3 are set as elevated or poetic speech). The Plain prints the book as prose, as the Leningrad Codex does; that layout is no evidence either way, since the Codex sets most prophetic poetry as prose too. The repeated formula 'But you say' opens eight of the people's objections.
Language
Hebrew, in a plain prose style with a foreign loan word, pechah 'governor' (1:8), the usual Persian-period term for a province's ruler.
Length
4 chapters in English, 55 verses (14, 17, 18, 6). The Hebrew has 3 chapters and the same 55 verses (14, 17, 24).
Verse numbers

English 4:1-6 is Hebrew 3:19-24, so Hebrew Malachi has three chapters. This site uses the English numbers. The Greek (Swete's text) starts its chapter 4 with the last words of English 3:18, and puts the Moses verse last: its 4:4-6 are English 4:5, 4:6 and 4:4.
Place in the Bible

The twelfth of the Twelve in the Hebrew and the Greek orders, and the last of the Latter Prophets in the Hebrew Bible. In Protestant and most Catholic Bibles it is the last book of the Old Testament, and Matthew follows.
Lenses

History (H), Critical (C), Jewish tradition (J) and Christian (X) apply to the whole book. The Still-to-come lens (F) applies only to 3:1-5 and 4:1-6, the coming of the Lord to his temple, the day, and Elijah.
Witnesses read

The Leningrad Codex (the base text); the Septuagint in Swete's edition; the Dead Sea scrolls 4QXIIa (4Q76), which preserves parts of 2:10-4:6, and 4QXIIc (4Q78), which preserves parts of 3:6-7, read in the Abegg, Bowley and Cook transcription. 4QXIIc agrees with the Masoretic Text in the words that are visible (see the note at 3:6). The printout lists no other scroll for Malachi, and no scroll for chapter 1 or 2:1-9. The Latin Vulgate is cited from Jerome's text. The auto-detected variants list for Malachi is empty; that is a fact about the auto file, not a claim that the witnesses agree, and the variants here were found by hand from the Greek and the scroll printouts.
authorship: The prophet Malachi spoke these words. Jewish tradition counts him with Haggai and Zechariah as one of the last prophets; the Talmud says the Holy Spirit left Israel after them (Yoma 9b). The Targum Jonathan identifies him with Ezra the scribe, and Jerome also discusses that identification. The Talmud (Megillah 15a) records three views: that he was Mordecai, that he was Ezra, and that Malachi was his real name.

'Malachi' (mal'akhi) is the Hebrew for 'my messenger' (3:1). The Greek reads 'by the hand of his messenger' (1:1), and the book gives no father, town or king, unlike Haggai or Zechariah. Many scholars think the heading is an editor's invention drawn from 3:1, as the two oracles of Zechariah 9-14 are also anonymous. Others think it is a real shortened name.

The book is a unity of six disputations by one writer, with a later epilogue (4:4-6) and perhaps small glosses (2:11-12; 3:1b-4). The three oracles headed massa' (Zechariah 9:1; 12:1; Malachi 1:1) suggest to some editors of the Twelve that Zechariah 9-14 and Malachi once formed a collection. Others hold that the book is a single composition from the middle Persian period.

audience.to: The priests and people of the Persian province of Judah, a poor farming community of a few tens of thousands around Jerusalem, whose Temple had been finished for some decades. The priests are addressed directly (1:6-2:9), the men of the community on marriage (2:10-16), and the whole people on justice, return and the tithe (2:17-3:12), with a word to the faithful (3:16-18).
audience.why: To answer a community's doubts about God. They asked how he loved them, where the God of justice was, how to return, and what was the use of serving him. Malachi answers each with the covenant: God's love shown in Edom's ruin, his claim to honest worship, the marriage covenant, his coming judgment, the tithe as the sign of return, and a record kept for the faithful. Knowing the audience matters: the book does not attack the Temple but asks the priests to run it as the law says; its 'tithe' passage is a call to feed the Temple's servants, with a promise of harvest to the whole community; and its harsh words about marriage were spoken to men with the power to send a wife away.
views: A Persian-period community, before Nehemiah's second term
A common view: the book was spoken and written between about 480 and 450 BC, after the Temple's completion and before Ezra and Nehemiah's reforms had taken hold.
The time of Nehemiah's second term
Others set it close to Nehemiah 13 (about 432 BC), because the abuses of tithes, priests and mixed marriage are the same.
The last form of the book, with its epilogue, was shaped for readers of the whole collection, who would hear 4:4-6 as the end of the Prophets.

outline: First dispute: the LORD's love; Jacob and Esau; Edom's ruin
Second dispute: the priests despise the LORD's name; polluted offerings; the pure offering among the nations; the covenant with Levi
Third dispute: betrayal in Judah; the foreign god's daughter; the wife of your youth; 'he hates sending away'
Fourth dispute: 'Where is the God of justice?'; the messenger; the refiner's fire; judgment on the guilty
Fifth dispute: 'Return to me'; robbing God in the tithe and the contribution; the open windows of heaven
Sixth dispute: 'Serving God is worthless'; the scroll of remembrance; the day that burns and the sun that heals
Epilogue: remember Moses; Elijah will come

lenses.name: History
lenses.desc: Reads the book against Persian-period Judah: the province of Yehud and its governor, the Temple finished about 515 BC and its priests, the ruin of Edom, the tithe and the Levites of Nehemiah 13, the marriage questions of Ezra 9-10. It asks what the book shows about worship and daily life after the rebuilding, and where it fits between Haggai, Zechariah and Nehemiah.

lenses.name: Critical
lenses.desc: Asks about the book's form (the disputation), its date and unity, the identity of 'Malachi', the relation of priests and Levites, the hard text of 2:11-16 and the Greek, Latin and Dead Sea variants, the literary link with Zechariah 9-14 and the Twelve, and the possible editorial nature of 4:4-6.

lenses.name: Jewish tradition
lenses.desc: Reads Malachi as Jews have read it: Rashi and the Targum Jonathan; the Talmud on divorce (Gittin 90), on the sun of 4:2 (Avodah Zarah 3b-4a) and on Elijah (Eduyot 8:7); the haftarot (Toledot, Shabbat HaGadol); the practice of repeating the last verse but one.

lenses.name: Christian
lenses.desc: Reads Malachi as the church has: the fathers (Justin, Irenaeus, Augustine, Jerome), the Reformers (Luther, Calvin), the New Testament's use of 1:2-3, 3:1 and 4:5-6 for John the Baptist and Christ, and the lectionaries. The churches disagree on election, the pure offering, divorce, the tithe and Elijah; the cards show their differences.

lenses.name: Still to come
lenses.desc: For 3:1-5 and 4:1-6 only: readers who hold that the coming of the Lord to his temple, the cleansing of Levi, the burning day and the return of Elijah are still future (Jewish messianic readers and futurist Christians), against those who hold they were fulfilled in the first century.

sections.b:
The book is a set of six arguments, each in three beats. The LORD makes a charge or a claim. The people object: "But you say, 'How have you loved us?'" The LORD answers. The same pattern runs through the Plain with the same English each time: "But you say." Reading the book as a courtroom lets the reader hear the people's own words, which are quoted back to them. The objections show what a discouraged Persian-period community was thinking: God does not love us, the altar is not worth much, evildoers do well, serving God is pointless.

Three words carry the book. 'Name' appears ten times (1:6, 11, 14; 2:2, 5; 3:16; 4:2): the LORD's name is despised by priests and great among the nations. 'Messenger' ties the title (1:1), the priest (2:7) and the coming figure (3:1). 'Betray' runs through 2:10-16. The Plain keeps one English for each of these.

The book names no king and no date. It speaks of a governor (1:8), a working Temple with its offerings (1:7-14; 3:10), priests who teach (2:1-9), Edom's ruin (1:3-4) and a community that includes men who marry women of other faiths (2:11). That puts it after about 515 BC and in the Persian period. Within that period three positions are held. One puts it about 480-450 BC, before the reforms of Ezra and Nehemiah, as several commentators do. One puts it close to Nehemiah's second term, about 432 BC, because of the shared problems (Nehemiah 13:4-31). A third treats the book as made in stages, with an epilogue added when the Twelve were put together. No decisive evidence settles it.

Malachi does not name the cause of Edom's ruin, and excavation does not simply show one: major Edomite sites stayed occupied into the Persian period (see the note on 1:3). The mention of the governor shows only that the province was ruled by an appointed official, as in Nehemiah 5:14-18.

The first long dispute is with the priests (1:6-2:9). They accept blind, lame and stolen animals against the law of Leviticus 22:17-25, call the altar's food something to look down on, and teach with partiality. The LORD holds up the covenant with Levi, which gave life and peace and made a priest the LORD's messenger (2:5-7), and says the priests have ruined it. Malachi writes 'priests' and 'Levi' as if one body, like Deuteronomy's 'Levite priests'; Ezra and Nehemiah keep Aaron's family and the Levites apart. Whether the book reflects a quarrel between them is disputed. The word 'teaching' (torah) is the priests' spoken ruling in 2:6-9 and the law of Moses in 4:4.

The opening dispute ('How have you loved us?') is answered by pointing to two brothers. Jacob's descendants are in their land and Edom's mountains are a waste. The words 'I hated' mean 'I did not choose', a covenant idiom (Genesis 29:30-33; Deuteronomy 21:15-17). Malachi speaks of nations, the Edom of the Persian period and Israel. Paul uses the line in Romans 9:13 to argue about God's free choice, and the churches read that use differently (see the card). A fair reading keeps the two questions apart: what Malachi says about two peoples, and what Paul does with it.

Malachi 2:10-16 is the hardest passage. The charge is betrayal (bagad, five times): of a brother, of the LORD's holy place by marrying 'the daughter of a foreign god', and of 'the wife of your youth'. Three readings are held. The men divorced Judean wives to marry foreign women; the marriage language is a picture of Judah's idolatry; or the passage is about marriage itself. Verse 16 has four readings (see the note and variant). The Plain gives the Hebrew as it stands, 'he hates sending away'. The Greek and the Latin read it as 'if you hate her, send her away', as do Rashi and the Targum Jonathan, and the Dead Sea scroll 4QXIIa visibly has the first words of that reading. Whichever is original, the next line is plain: 'So guard yourselves in your spirit, and do not betray.'

3:6-12 is the passage most often quoted from Malachi. The people have kept back the tithe and the contribution, and the Levites and priests have no food (compare Nehemiah 13:10-13). The LORD invites a test: bring the whole tithe, and see whether he will open the windows of the sky. The blessing is rain and harvest, the opposite of the locust and drought in Haggai 1:10-11. A popular teaching, the prosperity gospel, takes the verse as a promise that gifts return as money to the giver. The Hebrew addresses a nation and promises the covenant blessing of crops, and the storehouse fed the Temple's servants. Churches differ on whether Christians owe a tithe; see the card.

sections.h: The messenger, the day and Elijah
sections.b: 3:1 promises a messenger who clears the road before the LORD, and then the Lord's sudden coming to his temple, with 'the messenger of the covenant'. The Gospels read the messenger as John the Baptist (Matthew 11:10-14; Mark 1:2; Luke 7:27). 4:5-6 promises Elijah before the great and awesome day, a phrase also used in Joel 2:31. The book's last verse ends on a threat (the ban), and Jewish reading practice repeats the verse before it so as to end on the day. Both Jews and Christians have read 4:1-2 of the sun that burns the wicked and heals the righteous.

sections.h: The end of the Twelve and the Prophets
sections.b: 4:4-6 joins the Prophets to the law of Moses (Horeb, the rules and rulings of Deuteronomy) and looks beyond them to Elijah. Some read it as a closing note to the Twelve or to the whole Prophets. In the Hebrew Bible the Writings follow; in Protestant and most Catholic Bibles Matthew follows, and the New Testament's first prophecy of John takes up the words. The Septuagint puts the Moses verse last. The order of books creates different endings, but that is a reading of the canon, not a teaching of Malachi.

Jewish tradition reads 1:1-2:7 on the Sabbath of Jacob and Esau (Toledot) and 3:4-24 (Hebrew) before Passover, with Elijah's cup. Christian tradition reads 1:11 of the Eucharist (the Didache, Justin, Irenaeus, Trent), 3:1 and 4:5 of John, 4:2 of Christ. Handel's Messiah sets 3:1-3 as a bass aria. These are receptions. The Plain translates the Hebrew and keeps them in the notes and cards.

spec.title: Claude's theory: the book is built on three words, 'name', 'messenger' and 'betray'
spec.body: My reading is that Malachi is organized by three repeated Hebrew words that the Plain keeps in one English each. 'Name' (shem) occurs ten times and opens and closes the argument about worship: the priests despise it (1:6), the nations honor it (1:11, 14), the faithful fear it (4:2). 'Messenger' (mal'akh) turns the prophet's own name or title (1:1) into the priest (2:7), the forerunner (3:1) and the messenger of the covenant (3:1). 'Betray' (bagad) turns a dispute about marriage into a dispute about covenant (2:10-16). If a hearer heard these three words come back, the book would feel like one argument and not six. The claim that these three words organize the whole book is mine.

prompts: A hand-drawn scroll picture in ink and ochre: two hill countries side by side, one with terraced fields and a small walled city, the other with broken stone walls and jackals among the ruins, a pair of twin figures in the clouds above them. Cave-drawing animals, soft torn parchment edges, no hard rectangle.

A sketch on aged papyrus in a mix of ancient manuscript style and modern line art: a priest at a stone altar with a blind sheep and a limping goat waiting, a Persian official in robes in the doorway with folded arms. Soft uneven borders.

A cave-painting style picture on a scroll of a silversmith sitting at a crucible of glowing metal beside a cloth-washer treading a garment in a stone trough, red and ochre earth colors, edges fading like old vellum.

A manuscript-and-modern-art illustration of a rising sun with long feathered rays like wings, calves leaping out of a stall into a field below, ink, ochre and indigo, rough sketched edges, no square border.

A hand-drawn picture of a small group of people in simple robes talking together in a courtyard while above them an open scroll unrolls with their names, Hebrew letters in the margin, soft parchment texture.
reading: The fullest recent commentary: text, Persian background and a long discussion of the disputation form.
Beth Glazier-McDonald, Malachi: The Divine Messenger (SBL Dissertation Series 98, 1987)
A close study of the Hebrew and the book's themes, with a defense of its unity.
Pieter A. Verhoef, The Books of Haggai and Malachi (NICOT, 1987)
A conservative commentary with careful treatment of the date and the tithe.
David L. Petersen, Zechariah 9-14 and Malachi (Old Testament Library, 1995)
Reads the two together as the end of the Twelve.
Julia M. O'Brien, Priest and Levite in Malachi (SBL Dissertation Series 121, 1990)
On the priest-Levite question that runs through the book.
Gordon P. Hugenberger, Marriage as a Covenant (Supplements to Vetus Testamentum 52, 1994)
A study of marriage as covenant, with a long discussion of Malachi 2:14.
Adrian Graffy, A Prophet Confronts His People (Analecta Biblica 104, 1984)
On the disputation speech in the prophets.
